contextBoundaryNote: Events and statutes after 1588 lie outside this specification; Edexcel Option B4 strictly examines Early Elizabethan England from 1558 to 1588.

root.label: Elizabethan England, 1558–88
root.gloss: Thirty years of Elizabethan monarchy, religious settlement, Catholic plots, Anglo-Spanish war, social change, and Atlantic exploration from accession in 1558 to the 1588 Armada.

children.label: KT1: Queen, Govt & Religion
children.gloss: Key topic 1: Queen, government and religion, 1558–69 — Elizabeth’s accession, the 1559 Religious Settlement, Puritan and Catholic challenges, and Mary, Queen of Scots.

children.label: 1.1 Elizabeth's Accession
children.gloss: 16m Essay Lens: Legitimacy, gender & religious divisions at home vs £300,000 Crown debt & the French threat via Scotland as Elizabeth's gravest problem in 1558.

children.label: Society & Government in 1558
children.gloss: Elizabethan England in 1558 governed a hierarchical society through the Royal Court, Privy Council, patronage, Parliament, and unpaid county Justices of the Peace.

children.label: 19-Man Privy Council & Patronage
children.detail: Elizabeth cut Mary I’s council to 19 trusted advisers and used offices and monopolies to bind rival nobles.
children.gloss: Elizabeth cut Mary I’s council to 19 trusted advisers and used offices and monopolies to bind rival nobles.

children.label: No Army or Paid Police Force
children.detail: Lacking troops or police, the Crown relied on Lords Lieutenant and gentry Justices of the Peace in every shire.
children.gloss: Lacking troops or police, the Crown relied on Lords Lieutenant and gentry Justices of the Peace in every shire.

children.label: Parliament Held Tax Leverage
children.detail: Extraordinary war taxation needed House of Commons consent, letting MPs pressure Elizabeth over marriage and faith.
children.gloss: Extraordinary war taxation needed House of Commons consent, letting MPs pressure Elizabeth over marriage and faith.

children.label: Royal Prerogative Kept Control
children.detail: Guided by Principal Secretary William Cecil, Elizabeth summoned Parliament rarely and silenced forbidden debates.
children.gloss: Guided by Principal Secretary William Cecil, Elizabeth summoned Parliament rarely and silenced forbidden debates.

children.label: Virgin Queen, Legitimacy & Gender
children.gloss: Celebrated as the Virgin Queen, Elizabeth used her shrewd character and strengths to overcome doubts over her legitimacy, gender, and marriage.

children.label: Anne Boleyn & 1536 Succession Act
children.detail: Catholics rejected Henry VIII’s 1533 marriage to Anne Boleyn, viewing Elizabeth as illegitimate and unfit to rule.
children.gloss: Catholics rejected Henry VIII’s 1533 marriage to Anne Boleyn, viewing Elizabeth as illegitimate and unfit to rule.

children.label: Patriarchal Fear of Female Rule
children.detail: Sixteenth-century society doubted a solo queen could lead armies, while Mary I’s harsh reign worsened mistrust.
children.gloss: Sixteenth-century society doubted a solo queen could lead armies, while Mary I’s harsh reign worsened mistrust.

children.label: No Heir Risked Dynastic Civil War
children.detail: Staying unwed left England without a Protestant child, so sudden royal illness risked igniting civil conflict.
children.gloss: Staying unwed left England without a Protestant child, so sudden royal illness risked igniting civil conflict.

children.label: Humanist Strengths & Unwed Tact
children.detail: Fluent in six languages, Elizabeth stayed unwed so neither a foreign prince nor an English peer split her court.
children.gloss: Fluent in six languages, Elizabeth stayed unwed so neither a foreign prince nor an English peer split her court.

children.label: Finance, Religion & French Threat
children.gloss: Challenges at home and from abroad included severe financial weaknesses, deep religious divisions, and the French threat via Calais and Scotland.

children.label: £300,000 Debt & Antwerp Loans
children.detail: Ordinary Crown income was £286,000 while Mary’s French war left heavy debts borrowed at 14% interest in Antwerp.
children.gloss: Ordinary Crown income was £286,000 while Mary’s French war left heavy debts borrowed at 14% interest in Antwerp.

children.label: Auld Alliance & Loss of Calais
children.detail: France held Calais from January 1558 and garrisoned Scotland, where Catholic Mary Stuart claimed England’s crown.
children.gloss: France held Calais from January 1558 and garrisoned Scotland, where Catholic Mary Stuart claimed England’s crown.

children.label: Franco-Scottish Invasion Danger
children.detail: Encirclement on two fronts while the Treasury was bankrupt left southern ports and the Scottish border exposed.
children.gloss: Encirclement on two fronts while the Treasury was bankrupt left southern ports and the Scottish border exposed.

children.label: 1559 Cateau-Cambrésis Ended War
children.detail: Peace with France and Cecil’s thrift eased foreign danger faster than England’s deep Catholic-Protestant split.
children.gloss: Peace with France and Cecil’s thrift eased foreign danger faster than England’s deep Catholic-Protestant split.

children.label: 1.2 Religious Settlement
children.gloss: 16m Essay Lens: Broadly accepted 'middle way' securing peaceful parish conformity vs uneasy compromise opposed by Marian bishops and zealous Puritans.

children.label: Acts of Supremacy & Uniformity
children.gloss: Core features of Elizabeth's religious settlement in 1559 made her Supreme Governor and enforced a compromise English Book of Common Prayer.

children.label: Supreme Governor & Prayer Book
children.detail: Supremacy ended papal rule under a mild title, while Uniformity set an English prayer book and 12d recusant fines.
children.gloss: Supremacy ended papal rule under a mild title, while Uniformity set an English prayer book and 12d recusant fines.

children.label: Bridged Bitter Religious Divide
children.detail: Fusing 1549 and 1552 communion words let traditionalists and Protestants share worship without sparking civil war.
children.gloss: Fusing 1549 and 1552 communion words let traditionalists and Protestants share worship without sparking civil war.

children.label: 8,000 Parish Clergy Took the Oath
children.detail: Keeping vestments and mild language won wide acceptance, as nearly all 8,000 local vicars swore royal allegiance.
children.gloss: Keeping vestments and mild language won wide acceptance, as nearly all 8,000 local vicars swore royal allegiance.

children.label: 26 of 27 Marian Bishops Refused
children.detail: Catholic bishops in the Lords fought the bills and lost their sees, while returning Marian exiles hated vestments.
children.gloss: Catholic bishops in the Lords fought the bills and lost their sees, while returning Marian exiles hated vestments.

children.label: Injunctions & 1559 Visitations
children.gloss: Fifty-seven Royal Injunctions and nationwide visitations enforced Elizabeth's religious settlement (1559), shaping its parish features and impact.

children.label: 57 Injunctions & English Bibles
children.detail: Cecil ordered every church to display an English Bible, ban pilgrimages and fake miracles, and license preachers.
children.gloss: Cecil ordered every church to display an English Bible, ban pilgrimages and fake miracles, and license preachers.

children.label: Checked Compliance Across Shires
children.detail: 125 royal commissioners inspected every diocese in autumn 1559 to remove Catholic statues and administer the Oath.
children.gloss: 125 royal commissioners inspected every diocese in autumn 1559 to remove Catholic statues and administer the Oath.

children.label: Only 400 Priests Lost Livings
children.detail: Few dismissals let rural parishes keep familiar vicars, avoiding the armed religious revolts seen under Edward VI.
children.gloss: Few dismissals let rural parishes keep familiar vicars, avoiding the armed religious revolts seen under Edward VI.

children.label: Northern Gentry Hid Old Rituals
children.detail: Many conservative northern parishes dragged their feet removing altars and quietly skipped fining absent Catholics.
children.gloss: Many conservative northern parishes dragged their feet removing altars and quietly skipped fining absent Catholics.

children.label: Church of England in Society
children.gloss: The Church of England played a vital role in society, preaching royal loyalty, running moral courts, and organising village poor relief.

children.label: Church Courts & Parish Pulpits
children.detail: Church courts judged wills, slander, and sabbath-breaking while parish vicars read royal proclamations on Sundays.
children.gloss: Church courts judged wills, slander, and sabbath-breaking while parish vicars read royal proclamations on Sundays.

children.label: Maintained Rural Order & Welfare
children.detail: In mostly illiterate villages, licensed sermons taught obedience while churchwardens collected alms for local poor.
children.gloss: In mostly illiterate villages, licensed sermons taught obedience while churchwardens collected alms for local poor.

children.label: Embedded Crown Rule in Parishes
children.detail: Controlling bishoprics, preaching licences, and midwifery or schoolmaster permits anchored Tudor rule nationwide.
children.gloss: Controlling bishoprics, preaching licences, and midwifery or schoolmaster permits anchored Tudor rule nationwide.

children.label: Shortage of Educated Preachers
children.detail: Many rural parishes lacked university-trained Protestant clergy, relying instead on printed Book of Homilies texts.
children.gloss: Many rural parishes lacked university-trained Protestant clergy, relying instead on printed Book of Homilies texts.

children.label: 1.3 Religious Challenges
children.gloss: 16m Essay Lens: Domestic Puritan crucifix & vestment defiance vs Catholic nobility, the Papacy & Spanish armies in Flanders as the greater threat.

children.label: Puritan Crucifix & Vestment Clash
children.gloss: The scope and impact of the Puritan challenge centred on crucifixes and vestments until Parker sacked 37 London ministers in 1566.

children.label: Surplice & Parker Advertisements
children.detail: Puritans rejected white linen surplices as popish rags until Archbishop Parker enforced strict dress rules in 1566.
children.gloss: Puritans rejected white linen surplices as popish rags until Archbishop Parker enforced strict dress rules in 1566.

children.label: Geneva Exiles Wanted Pure Worship
children.detail: Returning Calvinists wanted to strip stained glass, organs, kneeling, and silver crucifixes from parish worship.
children.gloss: Returning Calvinists wanted to strip stained glass, organs, kneeling, and silver crucifixes from parish worship.

children.label: Forced Royal Crucifix Concession
children.detail: Bishops threatened resignation over the Royal Chapel crucifix, and 1563 Convocation missed reform by a single vote.
children.gloss: Bishops threatened resignation over the Royal Chapel crucifix, and 1563 Convocation missed reform by a single vote.

children.label: No Noble Backing or Rival Monarch
children.detail: When 37 London clergy lost their posts in 1566, most Puritans conformed rather than destabilise a Protestant Queen.
children.gloss: When 37 London clergy lost their posts in 1566, most Puritans conformed rather than destabilise a Protestant Queen.

children.label: Catholic Nobility & the Papacy
children.gloss: The scope and impact of the Catholic challenge involved northern nobility, gentry Church Papists, and the Papacy under Counter-Reformation popes.

children.label: Church Papists & Recusant Gentry
children.detail: Northern Catholics attended Sunday worship to avoid 12d fines while hearing private Latin Mass inside manor homes.
children.gloss: Northern Catholics attended Sunday worship to avoid 12d fines while hearing private Latin Mass inside manor homes.

children.label: Northern Earls Resented Lost Sway
children.detail: Traditional Catholic earls like Northumberland lost court influence to Protestant newcomers such as William Cecil.
children.gloss: Traditional Catholic earls like Northumberland lost court influence to Protestant newcomers such as William Cecil.

children.label: 1566 Papal Ban & Douai Seminary
children.detail: Pope Pius V barred Catholics from Anglican church in 1566 and William Allen opened Douai in 1568 to train priests.
children.gloss: Pope Pius V barred Catholics from Anglican church in 1566 and William Allen opened Douai in 1568 to train priests.

children.label: Passive Majority in Early 1560s
children.detail: Pius IV delayed excommunication and Elizabeth avoided harsh penalties, keeping most Catholics quiet before 1569.
children.gloss: Pius IV delayed excommunication and Elizabeth avoided harsh penalties, keeping most Catholics quiet before 1569.

children.label: Foreign Powers, Alba & Flanders
children.gloss: Catholic foreign powers deepened the religious challenge when Spain sent Alba's army to Flanders in 1567 and Elizabeth seized the Genoese Loan.

children.label: Alba’s 10,000 Troops & Embargo
children.detail: Philip II sent 10,000 veterans under Alba to Flanders in 1567 and halted Antwerp trade after 1568 gold seizures.
children.gloss: Philip II sent 10,000 veterans under Alba to Flanders in 1567 and halted Antwerp trade after 1568 gold seizures.

children.label: Seizure of £85,000 Genoese Loan
children.detail: In November 1568 Elizabeth seized Italian-loaned gold sheltering in English ports to weaken Alba’s Flanders army.
children.gloss: In November 1568 Elizabeth seized Italian-loaned gold sheltering in English ports to weaken Alba’s Flanders army.

children.label: Catholic Army Across the Channel
children.detail: Alba’s ruthless Council of Troubles put veteran Spanish forces hours from Kent, alarming Elizabeth’s Privy Council.
children.gloss: Alba’s ruthless Council of Troubles put veteran Spanish forces hours from Kent, alarming Elizabeth’s Privy Council.

children.label: France & Spain Distracted Pre-1569
children.detail: Civil war after Elizabeth’s failed 1562 Le Havre expedition tied down France, while Dutch rebels occupied Spain.
children.gloss: Civil war after Elizabeth’s failed 1562 Le Havre expedition tied down France, while Dutch rebels occupied Spain.

children.label: 1.4 Mary, Queen of Scots
children.gloss: 16m Essay Lens: Mary Stuart’s legitimate Tudor Catholic claim & 1569 Norfolk marriage intrigue vs Elizabeth’s shrewd York Inquiry containment.

children.label: Mary's Claim & Flight to England
children.gloss: Catholic Mary, Queen of Scots held a strong legitimate claim to the English throne before Scottish rebellion forced her into England in May 1568.

children.label: Margaret Tudor Bloodline & Son
children.detail: Henry VIII’s Catholic great-niece Mary bore Prince James in 1566, making her Elizabeth’s clear heir presumptive.
children.gloss: Henry VIII’s Catholic great-niece Mary bore Prince James in 1566, making her Elizabeth’s clear heir presumptive.

children.label: Kirk o’ Field & Bothwell Scandal
children.detail: After husband Darnley’s 1567 murder and Mary’s hasty marriage to chief suspect Bothwell, Scottish lords rebelled.
children.gloss: After husband Darnley’s 1567 murder and Mary’s hasty marriage to chief suspect Bothwell, Scottish lords rebelled.

children.label: Living Catholic Alternative Queen
children.detail: Fleeing Lochleven into Cumbria in May 1568 placed a legitimate Catholic rival directly inside Elizabeth’s kingdom.
children.gloss: Fleeing Lochleven into Cumbria in May 1568 placed a legitimate Catholic rival directly inside Elizabeth’s kingdom.

children.label: Murder Scandal Tainted Reputation
children.detail: Forced abdication and rumours of adultery and murder alienated moderate English gentry and foreign Catholic courts.
children.gloss: Forced abdication and rumours of adultery and murder alienated moderate English gentry and foreign Catholic courts.

children.label: York Inquiry & 1569 Norfolk Plot
children.gloss: Relations between Elizabeth and Mary in 1568–69 centred on the Casket Letters inquiry, house arrest, and the secret Duke of Norfolk marriage plot.

children.label: Casket Letters & Not Proven Ruling
children.detail: At the 1568–69 York Inquiry, Regent Moray showed eight letters blaming Mary, ending in Cecil’s not proven ruling.
children.gloss: At the 1568–69 York Inquiry, Regent Moray showed eight letters blaming Mary, ending in Cecil’s not proven ruling.

children.label: Four Unacceptable Policy Options
children.detail: Restoring, returning, freeing, or trying an anointed monarch carried peril, so Elizabeth kept Mary under guard.
children.gloss: Restoring, returning, freeing, or trying an anointed monarch carried peril, so Elizabeth kept Mary under guard.

children.label: Sparked 1569 Norfolk Court Plot
children.detail: Plans to wed Mary to England’s richest peer, the Duke of Norfolk, drew northern Catholic earls toward armed revolt.
children.gloss: Plans to wed Mary to England’s richest peer, the Duke of Norfolk, drew northern Catholic earls toward armed revolt.

children.label: Dudley Confessed & Norfolk Jailed
children.detail: Robert Dudley confessed the secret wedding scheme in September 1569, letting Elizabeth lock Norfolk in the Tower.
children.gloss: Robert Dudley confessed the secret wedding scheme in September 1569, letting Elizabeth lock Norfolk in the Tower.

children.label: KT2: Challenges Home & Abroad
children.gloss: Key topic 2: Challenges to Elizabeth at home and abroad, 1569–88 — the Northern Earls, Catholic plots, Mary Stuart’s execution, war with Spain, and the 1588 Armada.

children.label: 2.1 Plots & Revolts at Home
children.gloss: 16m Essay Lens: Foreign-backed Ridolfi, Throckmorton & Babington plots and the 1569 Northern Revolt vs Walsingham’s spies & loyal English gentry.

children.label: Revolt of the Northern Earls
children.gloss: Reasons for and significance of the Revolt of the Northern Earls (1569–70) combined lost noble power, Catholicism, and Mary Stuart.

children.label: 4,600 Rebels & Durham Latin Mass
children.detail: Northumberland and Westmorland tore up Durham Cathedral’s English Bible and celebrated Mass with 4,600 armed men.
children.gloss: Northumberland and Westmorland tore up Durham Cathedral’s English Bible and celebrated Mass with 4,600 armed men.

children.label: Lost Court Power & Norfolk Arrest
children.detail: Resenting Protestant outsiders like Cecil and Pilkington, both earls panicked after Norfolk’s marriage plot failed.
children.gloss: Resenting Protestant outsiders like Cecil and Pilkington, both earls panicked after Norfolk’s marriage plot failed.

children.label: Only Major Armed Rising of Reign
children.detail: Marching south toward Tutbury forced Elizabeth to move Mary to Coventry and execute 450 rebels under martial law.
children.gloss: Marching south toward Tutbury forced Elizabeth to move Mary to Coventry and execute 450 rebels under martial law.

children.label: No Spanish Aid & Loyal Shires
children.detail: Alba’s troops never landed at Hartlepool, northern gentry stayed loyal, and a reshaped Northern Council took grip.
children.gloss: Alba’s troops never landed at Hartlepool, northern gentry stayed loyal, and a reshaped Northern Council took grip.

children.label: Bull, Ridolfi & Throckmorton Plots
children.gloss: Following Pius V’s 1570 papal bull, features and significance of the Ridolfi and Throckmorton plots linked Mary to Franco-Spanish invasion.

children.label: Ridolfi (1571) & Throckmorton (1583)
children.detail: Ridolfi sought 10,000 Alba soldiers, while Throckmorton planned a French Guise Sussex landing financed by Madrid.
children.gloss: Ridolfi sought 10,000 Alba soldiers, while Throckmorton planned a French Guise Sussex landing financed by Madrid.

children.label: 1570 Papal Bull Freed Allegiance
children.detail: Regnans in Excelsis excommunicated Elizabeth and ordered devout English Catholics to end their allegiance to her.
children.gloss: Regnans in Excelsis excommunicated Elizabeth and ordered devout English Catholics to end their allegiance to her.

children.label: Unified Foreign & Domestic Danger
children.detail: Ambassador Mendoza funded Throckmorton in London, prompting his expulsion and the 1584 Bond of Association.
children.gloss: Ambassador Mendoza funded Throckmorton in London, prompting his expulsion and the 1584 Bond of Association.

children.label: Intercepted Before Troops Sailed
children.detail: State intelligence foiled both plots early, executing Norfolk in 1572 and hiking recusancy fines to £20 in 1581.
children.gloss: State intelligence foiled both plots early, executing Norfolk in 1572 and hiking recusancy fines to £20 in 1581.

children.label: Walsingham, Spies & Babington Plot
children.gloss: Features and significance of the Babington Plot (1586) showed how Francis Walsingham and the use of spies trapped Mary Stuart.

children.label: Beer-Barrel Ciphers & Phelippes
children.detail: Double agent Gilbert Gifford routed Chartley beer-barrel ciphers to codebreaker Thomas Phelippes for Walsingham.
children.gloss: Double agent Gilbert Gifford routed Chartley beer-barrel ciphers to codebreaker Thomas Phelippes for Walsingham.

children.label: 60,000-Man Invasion & Regicide Plan
children.detail: Anthony Babington and six gentlemen plotted to assassinate Elizabeth and rescue Mary alongside foreign invasion.
children.gloss: Anthony Babington and six gentlemen plotted to assassinate Elizabeth and rescue Mary alongside foreign invasion.

children.label: Proved Mary Backed Assassination
children.detail: Mary’s deciphered 17 July 1586 letter endorsing Elizabeth’s murder gave commissioners hard treason proof at last.
children.gloss: Mary’s deciphered 17 July 1586 letter endorsing Elizabeth’s murder gave commissioners hard treason proof at last.

children.label: Controlled Sting Never Near Action
children.detail: Walsingham monitored every message from start to finish, arresting Babington before any foreign ship left harbour.
children.gloss: Walsingham monitored every message from start to finish, arresting Babington before any foreign ship left harbour.

children.label: Mary Stuart's Execution in 1587
children.gloss: Reasons for and significance of Mary, Queen of Scots' execution in 1587 removed Catholic rebels' figurehead while provoking Philip II.

children.label: Fotheringhay Trial & Execution
children.detail: Convicted under the 1585 Safety Act, Mary was beheaded on 8 February 1587 wearing scarlet Catholic martyr robes.
children.gloss: Convicted under the 1585 Safety Act, Mary was beheaded on 8 February 1587 wearing scarlet Catholic martyr robes.

children.label: Anglo-Spanish War Ended Restraint
children.detail: Open war with Spain from 1585 and Babington’s regicide proof convinced councillors living Mary posed mortal peril.
children.gloss: Open war with Spain from 1585 and Babington’s regicide proof convinced councillors living Mary posed mortal peril.

children.label: Passed English Claim to Philip II
children.detail: Bypassing Protestant son James VI, Mary willed her English crown claim to Catholic Philip II, spurring invasion.
children.gloss: Bypassing Protestant son James VI, Mary willed her English crown claim to Catholic Philip II, spurring invasion.

children.label: Ended Domestic Plots & Kept James
children.detail: Executing Mary left English Catholics without a home rival, while James VI accepted Elizabeth’s letter of apology.
children.gloss: Executing Mary left English Catholics without a home rival, while James VI accepted Elizabeth’s letter of apology.

children.label: 2.2 Relations with Spain
children.gloss: 16m Essay Lens: Political & religious conflict over the Spanish Netherlands vs commercial rivalry & Francis Drake’s New World privateering.

children.label: Dutch Revolt & Spanish Rivalry
children.gloss: Political, religious, and commercial rivalry centred on Dutch Protestant rebels, Antwerp cloth exports, and Spanish troops in Flanders.

children.label: Sea Beggars & £100,000 Dutch Loan
children.detail: Expelled Sea Beggars seized Brielle in 1572, and Elizabeth lent £100,000 to Dutch rebels after 1576 Antwerp sack.
children.gloss: Expelled Sea Beggars seized Brielle in 1572, and Elizabeth lent £100,000 to Dutch rebels after 1576 Antwerp sack.

children.label: Channel Security & Antwerp Cloth
children.detail: Antwerp handled vital English wool exports, and Elizabeth feared a hostile Spanish army occupying North Sea ports.
children.gloss: Antwerp handled vital English wool exports, and Elizabeth feared a hostile Spanish army occupying North Sea ports.

children.label: Core Strategic Cause of Friction
children.detail: Philip II blamed covert English volunteers and loans for prolonging William of Orange’s Dutch Protestant revolt.
children.gloss: Philip II blamed covert English volunteers and loans for prolonging William of Orange’s Dutch Protestant revolt.

children.label: Elizabeth Refused Dutch Sovereignty
children.detail: Across the 1570s Elizabeth avoided formal war, using indirect loans while urging Philip to restore Dutch liberties.
children.gloss: Across the 1570s Elizabeth avoided formal war, using indirect loans while urging Philip to restore Dutch liberties.

children.label: Privateering & Drake's Raids
children.gloss: Commercial rivalry heightened the significance of privateering and the activities of Francis Drake across Spain’s New World empire.

children.label: Panama Silver & Cacafuego Plunder
children.detail: Drake raided Nombre de Dios in 1572 and seized £140,000 from Spain’s Pacific treasure ship Cacafuego in March 1579.
children.gloss: Drake raided Nombre de Dios in 1572 and seized £140,000 from Spain’s Pacific treasure ship Cacafuego in March 1579.

children.label: Spanish Monopoly & Crown Profit
children.detail: Barred from New World trade after San Juan de Ulúa, Elizabeth secretly backed raids returning £400,000 in 1580.
children.gloss: Barred from New World trade after San Juan de Ulúa, Elizabeth secretly backed raids returning £400,000 in 1580.

children.label: Cleared Debt & Enraged Philip II
children.detail: Crown plunder wiped out England’s debt while exposing unguarded Pacific ports and infuriating Spanish merchants.
children.gloss: Crown plunder wiped out England’s debt while exposing unguarded Pacific ports and infuriating Spanish merchants.

children.label: Did Not Trigger Open War in 1580
children.detail: Busy annexing Portugal in 1580, Philip II endured piracy until Elizabeth deployed soldiers to Flanders in 1585.
children.gloss: Busy annexing Portugal in 1580, Philip II endured piracy until Elizabeth deployed soldiers to Flanders in 1585.

children.label: Deptford Knighthood & Joinville
children.gloss: Drake’s 1581 knighthood, Parma’s Dutch reconquests, and the 1584 Treaty of Joinville destroyed indirect diplomacy with Madrid.

children.label: 1581 Deptford Sword & Alençon Aid
children.detail: Elizabeth had a French envoy knight Drake aboard the Golden Hind in April 1581 and funded Alençon’s Dutch campaign.
children.gloss: Elizabeth had a French envoy knight Drake aboard the Golden Hind in April 1581 and funded Alençon’s Dutch campaign.

children.label: Orange Killed & Joinville Signed
children.detail: William of Orange’s July 1584 murder and December’s Franco-Spanish Catholic treaty left Protestant England alone.
children.gloss: William of Orange’s July 1584 murder and December’s Franco-Spanish Catholic treaty left Protestant England alone.

children.label: Parma’s Advance Forced Action
children.detail: As the Duke of Parma besieged Antwerp, Dutch collapse threatened to hand Spain full control of the Channel coast.
children.gloss: As the Duke of Parma besieged Antwerp, Dutch collapse threatened to hand Spain full control of the Channel coast.

children.label: Alençon Strategy Failed First
children.detail: Backing the French Duke of Alençon failed by 1584, leaving reluctant English military intervention as last resort.
children.gloss: Backing the French Duke of Alençon failed by 1584, leaving reluctant English military intervention as last resort.

children.label: 2.3 Outbreak of War with Spain
children.gloss: 16m Essay Lens: Treaty of Nonsuch & Robert Dudley’s Dutch intervention vs Francis Drake’s 1587 Cadiz raid in shaping war with Spain.

children.label: Treaty of Nonsuch & Netherlands
children.gloss: Causes of deteriorating relations with Spain peaked through English direct involvement in the Netherlands under the 1585 Treaty of Nonsuch.

children.label: 7,400 Soldiers & Cautionary Ports
children.detail: Signed in August 1585, Nonsuch sent 7,400 English soldiers and garrisoned Flushing and Brielle as loan security.
children.gloss: Signed in August 1585, Nonsuch sent 7,400 English soldiers and garrisoned Flushing and Brielle as loan security.

children.label: Prevent Total Dutch Defeat by Parma
children.detail: After Antwerp fell and France allied with Spain at Joinville, only English troops could save the Dutch Revolt.
children.gloss: After Antwerp fell and France allied with Spain at Joinville, only English troops could save the Dutch Revolt.

children.label: Philip II Treated Nonsuch as War
children.detail: Sending a royal army into Philip’s rebel lands crossed a red line, making Madrid seize ships and arm an Armada.
children.gloss: Sending a royal army into Philip’s rebel lands crossed a red line, making Madrid seize ships and arm an Armada.

children.label: Half-Hearted Defensive War Aims
children.detail: Still hoping for compromise peace talks, Elizabeth denied her expedition enough siege artillery or pay for victory.
children.gloss: Still hoping for compromise peace talks, Elizabeth denied her expedition enough siege artillery or pay for victory.

children.label: Robert Dudley's Dutch Campaign
children.gloss: The actions of Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, in the Netherlands strained Anglo-Dutch trust yet denied Parma deep-water ports.

children.label: Governor-General & Deventer Loss
children.detail: Dudley accepted Governor-General in January 1586, while officers Stanley and Yorke betrayed Deventer and Zutphen.
children.gloss: Dudley accepted Governor-General in January 1586, while officers Stanley and Yorke betrayed Deventer and Zutphen.

children.label: Starved of Crown Pay & Supplies
children.detail: Angry that Dudley implied deposing Philip II, Elizabeth humiliated him publicly and withheld pay for hungry men.
children.gloss: Angry that Dudley implied deposing Philip II, Elizabeth humiliated him publicly and withheld pay for hungry men.

children.label: Held Deep-Water Port of Ostend
children.detail: Despite setbacks and recall in late 1587, Leicester slowed Parma and kept deep-water Ostend out of Spanish hands.
children.gloss: Despite setbacks and recall in late 1587, Leicester slowed Parma and kept deep-water Ostend out of Spanish hands.

children.label: Defections Wrecked Dutch Confidence
children.detail: Turncoats William Stanley and Rowland Yorke plus trade disputes with Dutch Estates left the alliance badly frayed.
children.gloss: Turncoats William Stanley and Rowland Yorke plus trade disputes with Dutch Estates left the alliance badly frayed.

children.label: Drake's Raid on Cadiz, April 1587
children.gloss: Francis Drake led the raid on Cadiz — 'Singeing the King of Spain's beard' — burning ships and seasoned barrel staves.

children.label: 30 Ships Burned & Barrel Staves
children.detail: Leading 24 warships into Cadiz in April 1587, Drake burned 30 ships plus seasoned oak staves off Cape St Vincent.
children.gloss: Leading 24 warships into Cadiz in April 1587, Drake burned 30 ships plus seasoned oak staves off Cape St Vincent.

children.label: Disrupt Invasion Fleet Assembly
children.detail: Warned by Walsingham’s spies of vast Spanish preparations, Elizabeth sent Drake to strike Spain’s ships in harbour.
children.gloss: Warned by Walsingham’s spies of vast Spanish preparations, Elizabeth sent Drake to strike Spain’s ships in harbour.

children.label: Bought Vital Year & Ruined Casks
children.detail: Delaying Spain until 1588 bought defence time, while damp green pine casks turned Armada food and water foul.
children.gloss: Delaying Spain until 1588 bought defence time, while damp green pine casks turned Armada food and water foul.

children.label: Slowed Rather Than Stopped Spain
children.detail: Funded by New World silver and Pope Sixtus V, Philip II still launched 130 ships under Medina Sidonia in 1588.
children.gloss: Funded by New World silver and Pope Sixtus V, Philip II still launched 130 ships under Medina Sidonia in 1588.

children.label: 2.4 The Spanish Armada
children.gloss: 16m Essay Lens: English race-built galleons, Calais fireships & naval tactics vs flawed Spanish plans & the "Protestant Wind" storms.

children.label: Spanish Armada Invasion Plans
children.gloss: Spanish invasion plans ordered Medina Sidonia’s 130-ship Spanish Armada to meet Parma’s Flanders army and cross to Kent.

children.label: 130 Ships & 27,000 Parma Veterans
children.detail: Medina Sidonia’s 130 ships and 30,000 men sailed in crescent order to escort Parma’s 27,000 troops from Flanders.
children.gloss: Medina Sidonia’s 130 ships and 30,000 men sailed in crescent order to escort Parma’s 27,000 troops from Flanders.

children.label: Restore Catholicism & Stop Raids
children.detail: Philip II sought to avenge Mary Stuart, end Dutch intervention and piracy, and restore Catholic rule in England.
children.gloss: Philip II sought to avenge Mary Stuart, end Dutch intervention and piracy, and restore Catholic rule in England.

children.label: No Deep-Water Flanders Harbour
children.detail: Parma’s unarmed barges needed 48 hours to emerge from canals watched by Justin of Nassau’s nimble Dutch flyboats.
children.gloss: Parma’s unarmed barges needed 48 hours to emerge from canals watched by Justin of Nassau’s nimble Dutch flyboats.

children.label: Tight Crescent Held Up the Channel
children.detail: Disciplined Spanish wings shielded supply ships past Plymouth and the Isle of Wight with tiny losses before Calais.
children.gloss: Disciplined Spanish wings shielded supply ships past Plymouth and the Isle of Wight with tiny losses before Calais.

children.label: Calais Fireships & Gravelines
children.gloss: Key events of the Spanish Armada peaked on 7–8 August 1588 when Calais fireships broke Spain’s crescent before defeat at Gravelines.

children.label: 8 Fireships & 9-Hour Sea Battle
children.detail: Drifting eight pitch fireships into Calais on 7 August scattered Spain before fierce broadsides off Gravelines.
children.gloss: Drifting eight pitch fireships into Calais on 7 August scattered Spain before fierce broadsides off Gravelines.

children.label: Fear of Explosive Hell-Burners
children.detail: Dreading giant Antwerp bomb ships, panicked Spanish captains cut main anchor cables in darkness and broke order.
children.gloss: Dreading giant Antwerp bomb ships, panicked Spanish captains cut main anchor cables in darkness and broke order.

children.label: Gravelines Ruined Army Link-Up
children.detail: Closing within 100 yards on 8 August, English gunnery wrecked five galleons and drove Sidonia north past Flanders.
children.gloss: Closing within 100 yards on 8 August, English gunnery wrecked five galleons and drove Sidonia north past Flanders.

children.label: English Ships Ran Out of Shot
children.detail: Fireships burned zero hulls directly, and low powder and shot forced Howard to halt chase in the North Sea.
children.gloss: Fireships burned zero hulls directly, and low powder and shot forced Howard to halt chase in the North Sea.

children.label: Reasons for the English Victory
children.gloss: Reasons for the English victory combined race-built galleons, rapid gunnery, Howard and Drake’s tactics, and Atlantic gales.

children.label: Race-Built Galleons & Culverins
children.detail: Hawkins’s agile warships mounted four-wheeled bronze culverins firing three times faster than clumsy Spanish guns.
children.gloss: Hawkins’s agile warships mounted four-wheeled bronze culverins firing three times faster than clumsy Spanish guns.

children.label: Stand-Off Tactics Beat Boarding
children.detail: Keeping the windward gauge, Howard and Drake fired stand-off salvos and denied Spanish soldiers boarding hooks.
children.gloss: Keeping the windward gauge, Howard and Drake fired stand-off salvos and denied Spanish soldiers boarding hooks.

children.label: Naval Design & Tactics Won Battle
children.detail: Superior ship speed, gun carriages, and Calais fireships defeated invasion plans before autumn storms ever struck.
children.gloss: Superior ship speed, gun carriages, and Calais fireships defeated invasion plans before autumn storms ever struck.

children.label: Protestant Wind & Irish Shipwrecks
children.detail: Atlantic gales forced a Scottish-Irish retreat without anchors, wrecking 25+ ships so barely 67 reached Spain.
children.gloss: Atlantic gales forced a Scottish-Irish retreat without anchors, wrecking 25+ ships so barely 67 reached Spain.

children.label: KT3: Society & Exploration
children.gloss: Key topic 3: Elizabethan society in the Age of Exploration, 1558–88 — education and leisure, poverty and vagabondage, Drake’s circumnavigation, and Virginia.

children.label: 3.1 Education & Leisure
children.gloss: 16m Essay Lens: Expanding grammar schools & cross-class London playhouses vs persistent class and gender divides in literacy and sport.

children.label: Education in the Home & Schools
children.gloss: Education in the home under private tutors and in petty, dame, and town grammar schools raised gentry and merchant male literacy.

children.label: 72 New Grammar Schools & Tutors
children.detail: Nobles hired home tutors, while 72 grammar schools opened in the 1560s–70s teaching Latin, Greek, and scripture.
children.gloss: Nobles hired home tutors, while 72 grammar schools opened in the 1560s–70s teaching Latin, Greek, and scripture.

children.label: Humanism, Protestantism & Trade
children.detail: Protestants urged Bible reading, humanists prized classical learning, and merchants needed literate, numerate sons.
children.gloss: Protestants urged Bible reading, humanists prized classical learning, and merchants needed literate, numerate sons.

children.label: Male Literacy Reached 30% by 1580s
children.detail: Petty schools, grammar scholarships, and growing Oxford and Cambridge colleges lifted male literacy toward 30%.
children.gloss: Petty schools, grammar scholarships, and growing Oxford and Cambridge colleges lifted male literacy toward 30%.

children.label: Labourers & Girls Left Behind
children.detail: Rural children laboured from age six, universities barred women, and female literacy remained stuck near 10%.
children.gloss: Rural children laboured from age six, universities barred women, and female literacy remained stuck near 10%.

children.label: Elizabethan Sport & Pastimes
children.gloss: Elizabethan sport and pastimes reflected social rank between noble hunting or real tennis, parish folk football, and blood sports.

children.label: Deer Hunting vs Village Football
children.detail: Nobles hunted deer and played indoor real tennis, whereas labourers played rough, rule-free parish folk football.
children.gloss: Nobles hunted deer and played indoor real tennis, whereas labourers played rough, rule-free parish folk football.

children.label: Land Laws, Wealth & Spare Time
children.detail: Strict game laws reserved deer and hawks for landowners, whereas farmhands worked six days and played on holy days.
children.gloss: Strict game laws reserved deer and hawks for landowners, whereas farmhands worked six days and played on holy days.

children.label: Blood Sports Drew Every Class
children.detail: Southwark bear-baiting and cock-fighting rings drew Privy Councillors, gentry, and penny apprentices together.
children.gloss: Southwark bear-baiting and cock-fighting rings drew Privy Councillors, gentry, and penny apprentices together.

children.label: Separate Spaces Preserved Rank
children.detail: Even at shared baiting arenas, wealthy spectators sat in raised galleries apart from standing labourers in the pit.
children.gloss: Even at shared baiting arenas, wealthy spectators sat in raised galleries apart from standing labourers in the pit.

children.label: Growth of Elizabethan Theatre
children.gloss: Licensed acting companies and purpose-built London playhouses made the theatre thrive across social ranks despite Puritan opposition.

children.label: Burbage’s 1576 Theatre & 1d Yard
children.detail: James Burbage opened The Theatre in Shoreditch in 1576, where penny groundlings stood below covered gentry seats.
children.gloss: James Burbage opened The Theatre in Shoreditch in 1576, where penny groundlings stood below covered gentry seats.

children.label: Noble Patronage & Secular Plays
children.detail: Requiring noble licences in the 1572 Vagabonds Act created professional troupes like the Queen’s Men (1583).
children.gloss: Requiring noble licences in the 1572 Vagabonds Act created professional troupes like the Queen’s Men (1583).

children.label: 2,000-Strong Crowds & Royal Favour
children.detail: Vibrant secular comedies and histories packed 2,000 spectators into playhouses like the Curtain and Rose (1587).
children.gloss: Vibrant secular comedies and histories packed 2,000 spectators into playhouses like the Curtain and Rose (1587).

children.label: Puritan & City Plague Opposition
children.detail: London aldermen and Puritans barred playhouses inside city walls, blaming crowds for plague, crime, and sin.
children.gloss: London aldermen and Puritans barred playhouses inside city walls, blaming crowds for plague, crime, and sin.

children.label: 3.2 Problem of the Poor
children.gloss: 16m Essay Lens: 35% population growth, bad harvests & inflation vs sheep-farming enclosure & cloth slumps as the main cause of poverty.

children.label: Population, Inflation & Enclosure
children.gloss: Reasons for the increase in poverty and vagabondage during these years included population growth, inflation, bad harvests, and enclosure.

children.label: 3m to 4m Population & Sheep Land
children.detail: Population rose 35% to four million while landlords hedged village strips into sheep farms needing 90% less work.
children.gloss: Population rose 35% to four million while landlords hedged village strips into sheep farms needing 90% less work.

children.label: 80% Wool Exports & Harvest Slumps
children.detail: Booming wool exports tempted landlords to rack-rent and enclose, while 1573–77 wet harvests spiked grain prices.
children.gloss: Booming wool exports tempted landlords to rack-rent and enclose, while 1573–77 wet harvests spiked grain prices.

children.label: Population Outpaced Jobs & Food
children.detail: Surplus workers, 1563 Statute of Artificers wage caps, and coin-debasement inflation slashed real wages everywhere.
children.gloss: Surplus workers, 1563 Statute of Artificers wage caps, and coin-debasement inflation slashed real wages everywhere.

children.label: Enclosure & Embargoes Uprooted Men
children.detail: Rural evictions and Spanish Antwerp cloth embargoes pushed jobless farmhands and weavers onto shire roads.
children.gloss: Rural evictions and Spanish Antwerp cloth embargoes pushed jobless farmhands and weavers onto shire roads.

children.label: Impotent Poor vs Sturdy Beggars
children.gloss: Changing attitudes towards the poor separated deserving impotent poor from able-bodied sturdy beggars feared for crime and vagabondage.

children.label: Deserving Poor vs Harman’s Conmen
children.detail: Parishes aided sick or aged impotent poor, while Thomas Harman’s 1567 book exposed tricks by sturdy beggars.
children.gloss: Parishes aided sick or aged impotent poor, while Thomas Harman’s 1567 book exposed tricks by sturdy beggars.

children.label: Gentry Fear of Crime & Rebellion
children.detail: Lacking police, unpaid JPs feared masterless vagrants carried plague, stole property, and joined armed revolts.
children.gloss: Lacking police, unpaid JPs feared masterless vagrants carried plague, stole property, and joined armed revolts.

children.label: Recognised Genuine Unemployment
children.detail: Repeated cloth-trade slumps convinced MPs by 1576 that many able-bodied adults lacked work through no laziness.
children.gloss: Repeated cloth-trade slumps convinced MPs by 1576 that many able-bodied adults lacked work through no laziness.

children.label: Fear of Idleness Stayed Harsh
children.detail: Popular pamphlets and Puritan sermons still branded wandering vagrants as idle threats needing physical punishment.
children.gloss: Popular pamphlets and Puritan sermons still branded wandering vagrants as idle threats needing physical punishment.

children.label: 1572 & 1576 Poor Relief Policies
children.gloss: Government policies towards the poor combined compulsory poor rates and ear-boring in 1572 with parish work stocks and Bridewells in 1576.

children.label: Compulsory Poor Rate & Wool Work
children.detail: The 1572 Vagabonds Act taxed rich locals weekly, while the 1576 Act bought raw wool so jobless poor could spin.
children.gloss: The 1572 Vagabonds Act taxed rich locals weekly, while the 1576 Act bought raw wool so jobless poor could spin.

children.label: Voluntary Alms Failed After 1569
children.detail: Growing town poverty and post-1569 revolt fears pushed Parliament to replace voluntary alms with compulsory rates.
children.gloss: Growing town poverty and post-1569 revolt fears pushed Parliament to replace voluntary alms with compulsory rates.

children.label: National Parish Duty Established
children.detail: Taxing parishes and providing flax, hemp, and wool in 1576 created permanent local support for unemployed workers.
children.gloss: Taxing parishes and providing flax, hemp, and wool in 1576 created permanent local support for unemployed workers.

children.label: Whipping, Ear-Boring & Bridewells
children.detail: Fierce punishment remained: vagrants faced whipping, hot-iron ear boring, hanging, or hard labour in Bridewells.
children.gloss: Fierce punishment remained: vagrants faced whipping, hot-iron ear boring, hanging, or hard labour in Bridewells.

children.label: 3.3 Exploration & Discovery
children.gloss: 16m Essay Lens: Commercial trade expansion & anti-Spanish plunder vs new ship technology, navigation instruments & Mercator maps.

children.label: Ship Technology, Sailing & Maps
children.gloss: New technology on ships and open-sea sailing — race-built galleons, lateen sails, astrolabes, quadrants, and Mercator maps — enabled voyages.

children.label: Astrolabes, Quadrants & Mercator
children.detail: Sailors fixed latitude by astrolabe and quadrant while Mercator’s 1569 world grid map guided compass navigation.
children.gloss: Sailors fixed latitude by astrolabe and quadrant while Mercator’s 1569 world grid map guided compass navigation.

children.label: Atlantic Gales & Long Ocean Runs
children.detail: Hawkins’s race-built galleons combined square and lateen sails with bigger food holds and heavy culverin decks.
children.gloss: Hawkins’s race-built galleons combined square and lateen sails with bigger food holds and heavy culverin decks.

children.label: Made Transoceanic Voyages Viable
children.detail: Printed navigation manuals, compasses, and sleek galleon hulls let English crews survive long Pacific crossings.
children.gloss: Printed navigation manuals, compasses, and sleek galleon hulls let English crews survive long Pacific crossings.

children.label: Profit Motives Funded Shipyards
children.detail: Instruments made voyages safer, yet courtiers and merchants funded fleets only when lured by rich foreign profits.
children.gloss: Instruments made voyages safer, yet courtiers and merchants funded fleets only when lured by rich foreign profits.

children.label: Drive to Expand Overseas Trade
children.gloss: Factors prompting exploration included Antwerp cloth slumps and the merchant drive to expand trade via new companies and sea routes.

children.label: Muscovy, Levant & Arctic Quests
children.detail: Merchants traded Russian furs and Ottoman spices while Frobisher and Davis searched Arctic seas for Asian routes.
children.gloss: Merchants traded Russian furs and Ottoman spices while Frobisher and Davis searched Arctic seas for Asian routes.

children.label: Antwerp Collapse & Spanish Bans
children.detail: Spanish embargoes choked Antwerp wool exports and barred English ships from direct New World and Asian trade.
children.gloss: Spanish embargoes choked Antwerp wool exports and barred English ships from direct New World and Asian trade.

children.label: Joint-Stock Capital Drove Voyages
children.detail: Shared investor risk financed Eastland (1579), Levant (1581), and Hawkins’s 1562 Atlantic slave-trading voyages.
children.gloss: Shared investor risk financed Eastland (1579), Levant (1581), and Hawkins’s 1562 Atlantic slave-trading voyages.

children.label: Arctic Ice Blocked Asian Shortcut
children.detail: Northwest Passage expeditions (1576–87) failed in Baffin ice, making Spanish plunder richer than northern routes.
children.gloss: Northwest Passage expeditions (1576–87) failed in Baffin ice, making Spanish plunder richer than northern routes.

children.label: Drake's Circumnavigation, 1577–80
children.gloss: Reasons for and significance of Drake's circumnavigation of the globe included Spanish plunder, Nova Albion, and 4,700% profit.

children.label: Golden Hind, Nova Albion & Cloves
children.detail: Alone past Magellan, Golden Hind raided Peru, claimed California as Nova Albion, and traded for Moluccas cloves.
children.gloss: Alone past Magellan, Golden Hind raided Peru, claimed California as Nova Albion, and traded for Moluccas cloves.

children.label: Revenge & Secret Royal Investment
children.detail: Avenging Spain’s 1568 San Juan de Ulúa ambush, Elizabeth, Walsingham, and Leicester backed raids on Pacific silver.
children.gloss: Avenging Spain’s 1568 San Juan de Ulúa ambush, Elizabeth, Walsingham, and Leicester backed raids on Pacific silver.

children.label: 4,700% Profit & Global Prestige
children.detail: Returning £400,000 cleared Crown debt, paid 4,700% profit, and spurred Raleigh’s Virginia plans with sea charts.
children.gloss: Returning £400,000 cleared Crown debt, paid 4,700% profit, and spurred Raleigh’s Virginia plans with sea charts.

children.label: Four Ships Lost & War Hastened
children.detail: Four of five vessels were lost, and Elizabeth’s 1581 Deptford knighting pushed humiliated Philip II closer to war.
children.gloss: Four of five vessels were lost, and Elizabeth’s 1581 Deptford knighting pushed humiliated Philip II closer to war.

children.label: 3.4 Colonisation of Virginia
children.gloss: 16m Essay Lens: Late sailing, Tiger supply wreck & poor colonist skills vs Chief Wingina’s Secotan resistance & 1588 Armada delays.

children.label: Raleigh & Plans for Virginia
children.gloss: Causes of attempted colonisation of Virginia centred on Sir Walter Raleigh’s 1584 royal patent, Atlantic trade, and anti-Spanish bases.

children.label: 1584 Patent, Recon & Hakluyt Book
children.detail: Raleigh raised £40,000, sent Amadas and Barlowe to bring Manteo and Wanchese, and backed Hakluyt’s 1584 tract.
children.gloss: Raleigh raised £40,000, sent Amadas and Barlowe to bring Manteo and Wanchese, and backed Hakluyt’s 1584 tract.

children.label: Raid Spain & Replace European Goods
children.detail: Virginia offered an Atlantic base against Spanish ships plus timber, wine, and Native markets for English cloth.
children.gloss: Virginia offered an Atlantic base against Spanish ships plus timber, wine, and Native markets for English cloth.

children.label: Careful 1584 Prep & Algonquian Ties
children.detail: Learning Algonquian from Manteo with scientist Harriot and artist White gave Raleigh strong data before 1585.
children.gloss: Learning Algonquian from Manteo with scientist Harriot and artist White gave Raleigh strong data before 1585.

children.label: No Crown Cash & Raleigh Kept Home
children.detail: Denying Crown cash and barring Raleigh from sailing split leadership between rival commanders Grenville and Lane.
children.gloss: Denying Crown cash and barring Raleigh from sailing split leadership between rival commanders Grenville and Lane.

children.label: 1585 Roanoke Voyage & Tiger Wreck
children.gloss: Causes of failure of the first settlement in Virginia included late departure, poor colonist skills, and the Tiger shipwreck.

children.label: 107 Male Settlers & Ruined Seed
children.detail: Leaving late in April 1585 with 107 men, flagship Tiger grounded at Ocracoke and seawater ruined most seed corn.
children.gloss: Leaving late in April 1585 with 107 men, flagship Tiger grounded at Ocracoke and seawater ruined most seed corn.

children.label: Too Many Soldiers & Gold-Hunters
children.detail: Half the colonists were soldiers and proud gentlemen hunting quick gold rather than skilled farmers or craftsmen.
children.gloss: Half the colonists were soldiers and proud gentlemen hunting quick gold rather than skilled farmers or craftsmen.

children.label: Supply Loss Forced Native Reliance
children.detail: Missing spring planting and losing peas, salt, and gunpowder left Roanoke unable to feed itself over winter.
children.gloss: Missing spring planting and losing peas, salt, and gunpowder left Roanoke unable to feed itself over winter.

children.label: Secotan Traps Initially Fed Colony
children.detail: Even after the Tiger wreck, Algonquians shared maize and woven fish traps until English aggression wrecked trust.
children.gloss: Even after the Tiger wreck, Algonquians shared maize and woven fish traps until English aggression wrecked trust.

children.label: Secotan Conflict & 1587 Colony
children.gloss: Causes of failure in Virginia deepened when conflict with Chief Wingina wrecked the 1585–86 colony and the 1588 Armada stranded Roanoke.

children.label: Wingina Ambush & 1587 Lost Settlers
children.detail: Lane killed Secotan Chief Wingina in June 1586 before leaving with Drake; White’s 118 families arrived in 1587.
children.gloss: Lane killed Secotan Chief Wingina in June 1586 before leaving with Drake; White’s 118 families arrived in 1587.

children.label: Drought, Disease & Burned Village
children.detail: Grenville’s burning of Aquascogoc, European disease, and drought made Wingina halt maize trade with Lane’s fort.
children.gloss: Grenville’s burning of Aquascogoc, European disease, and drought made Wingina halt maize trade with Lane’s fort.

children.label: Native Hostility Doomed Roanoke
children.detail: Losing Algonquian food forced Lane’s 1586 evacuation and met John White’s 1587 families with immediate hostility.
children.gloss: Losing Algonquian food forced Lane’s 1586 evacuation and met John White’s 1587 families with immediate hostility.

children.label: 1588 Armada Blocked Relief Ships
children.detail: Keeping every English ship home against Spain’s 1588 Armada stopped John White returning with urgent supplies.
children.gloss: Keeping every English ship home against Spain’s 1588 Armada stopped John White returning with urgent supplies.
